newsitem.title: GERMANY: Computer age to revolutionise classroom - expert.
newsitem.headline: Computer age to revolutionise classroom - expert.

text.p: The computer age is set to explode traditional models of schooling, making rigid classrooms obsolete and creating a generation of skilled infant computer programmers, a U.S. education expert said Friday.

Seymour Papert, co-founder of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), told reporters at the Frankfurt Book Fair that computer-obsessed children and their parents would force schools to revolutionise their approach to education.
Timetables and age-streaming would ultimately be replaced by "communities" of children, actively engaged in computer-based projects and continually consulting their peers electronically.

"The current model of school is like the command economy in the Soviet Union. It was useful in the past only because there was no alternative. But why should we expect children to work in a way that we adults never would?," Papert said.

In the school of the future, traditional subject distinctions would disappear. Children would instead work on long term personal projects, solving problems from different disciplines, be it maths, art or history, as they arose.

"All these classifications we have now are absurd and people are not going to want to do that anymore. Children don't hate school now because it's hard, they hate it because it's boring," Papert said.

Papert said the MIT was running a project teaching eight and nine-year olds programming skills to enable them create their own personal computer games. The children were learning to programme 20 to 100 times faster than their peers, he said.
Papert, in Germany to advise on new software developments here, said most existing child education software was inadequate to cover future needs. More innovative products were needed.

"Most of what we have is totally ridiculous. It treats children like answering machines. But parents are getting more discriminating and software firms who are looking to the future will have real market niche," he said.
The Frankfurt Book Fair, open Oct 2-7, is emphasising multimedia projects, with over 2,000 exhibits. It is now the world's biggest electronic publishing trade fair.
